General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Architecturaldigest ↗ Open Full Page

23 Christmas Decoration Ideas, From Traditional Tartans to a Jewel-Toned Winter Wonderland

📅 25 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Seeing holiday decor get a modern-design makeover is my Roman Empire,” says home expert Julian Thomas.
  • But if you’re more of a traditionalist, you’ll find inspiration to fit your style here, too.
  • A dark and moody space shouldn’t stop you from merry decor for the holiday season—lean into it with your Christmas decorations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Seeing holiday decor get a modern-design makeover is my Roman Empire,” says home expert Julian Thomas. These Christmas decoration ideas will set a festive tone in any room of the house—and yes, it’s possible to deck your halls in an elevated way. “In the past, if you decorated for the holidays you had to sacrifice style and aesthetics for nostalgia and Christmas necessities,” he says. “Not any more. From silk tree skirts to Clivia marble stocking holders, Christmas decorations have never been chicer.”.

But if you’re more of a traditionalist, you’ll find inspiration to fit your style here, too. In fact, multiple design pros we spoke to mentioned that this year’s big trend is nostalgia (more on that below). With retro inspiration as well as upcoming takes on festive color palettes, plus creative Christmas garlands and interior design-friendly stockings, here are 23 Christmas decor ideas for all kinds of merrymakers.

A dark and moody space shouldn’t stop you from merry decor for the holiday season—lean into it with your Christmas decorations.

Recent findings suggest that “Red and green are traditional Christmas colors, but I love to break away from tradition a bit and use bright jewel tones to create a dramatic and sophisticated look for the holiday season,” states Annie Sloan, paint and color expert and creator of Chalk Paint. She is a fan of purple—once reserved for kings and emperors—for the holidays. “My Tyrian Plum Wall Paint is a rich, jewel-toned plum with maroon and red elements,” she says. “It works beautifully with metallics, fairy lights, and flickering candlelight to create a Christmas fit for the three kings!”.

Glass jars of gelt and dreidels set a stylish holiday vignette.

For an easy DIY project, fill glass jars with small holiday decor items, like dreidels or gold coins, as seen in this Hanukkah-adorned living room arranged by LA-based designer Ethan Charles Greenfeld of Ethan Charles Design. Pinecones, tiny Christmas ornaments, bows, or mini Santa figures would all make great options as well.

Centering your tree in the entryway sets a festive tone right away.

In a recent development, get more bang for your balsam by placing it in a spot in your living room that’s visible from other areas of the house—even better if you can see it from your home’s entryway. “I love making an impact with my tree and recommend putting it front and center if you can,” indicates designer Lauren Ashley of Lauren Ashley Experiences in Houston. “The tree is only up for a few weeks, so why not showcase it right at your entrance if there’s room?” Not only will guests get a peek at all your trimmings, you can enjoy the tree each time you come and go from your home.

Carry Christmas cheer throughout the house with wreaths and bows.

“I like to decorate the rooms we spend the most time in since Christmas decor just makes me so happy,” states lifestyle blogger and content creator Miyaeva Renae. “This year, I’m planning to decorate our living room, kitchen, bedroom, nursery, and even the bathrooms to bring that festive feeling throughout the house.” Here, Renae has wrapped kitchen cabinets in bows and placed mini wreaths on the backs of island chairs. Other small touches—like a wreath on the range hood, ribbon tied around a utensils jar, and a bowl filled with pinecones—add even more holiday cheer.

For those who leave gifts under the tree for a little while before Christmas day, it’s worth considering how the paper fits in with your decorative scheme.

This will inspire you to get your wrapping done early, and it gives your gift boxes another purpose: dressing up your living room before the big exchange on Christmas morning. “I love to make my own gift wrap,” Sloan says. “Buy cheap brown packing paper and paint it yourself with stripes, spots, or any design you fancy. Add contrasting ribbons and pile your gifts under the tree. Your gifts become part of your Christmas scheme. It’s stunning.” By making your own wrapping paper, you can also make sure it perfectly complements the rest of your decor.

Holiday-themed decals are a good—and renter-friendly—way to get your space looking festive.

For big impact without big effort, consider a high-quality wall sticker like the Victorian-inspired Christmas variety from Wallpick. “No tools are needed to apply Wallpick’s stickers, however I do recommend applying them to smooth walls for the best results,” says Wallpick’s founder Dina Jasmin. Use a wall sticker to frame your Christmas tree. Or, if a tree isn’t in the prepares, the sticker can serve as a focal point and place to gather presents.

A Christmas tree, garland, wreath, and throw pillows add some Christmas cheer to this otherwise calm, neutral bedroom.

According to recent reports, wake up in a winter wonderland by hanging a wreath above the bed and wrapping bed posts in a garland and string lights. Throw pillows featuring trees or snowflakes add a further festive touch—and if you really want to go all out, put a pre-lit Christmas tree in your bedroom as well. This year, Renae is even extending the Christmas home decor beyond the primary suite: “I usually don’t decorate our guest bedroom, but since we’ll have family staying with us this, I’m planning to add some holiday touches there too along with all of the bathrooms,” she says. “It’s such a fun way to make every space feel festive and welcoming.”.

What’s better than one Christmas tree in your entryway? Two.

“I love to host, so it’s not uncommon for friends and family to gather at my house throughout the season,” states Wendy Lau, Yale Home’s interior design consultant. While living rooms and dining areas may pull focus when it comes to Christmas decoration ideas, Lau greets guests with yuletide flair upon arrival: “One of my favorite places to decorate for the holidays is the entryway.” She uses a smart lock programmed with custom codes to help guests feel right at home, so they can see themselves in and be dazzled by eye-catching visuals like “greenery and twinkle lights—always a charming sight. I also like to drape garlands over the doorway and hang massive wreaths with a jolly red bow out front.” A holiday-themed doormat at the front door as part of the porch decor completes the festive first impression.

This felt ball garland is a creative departure from the traditional greenery.

According to recent reports, hang strings of felt balls, dried oranges, yarn tassels, or stars cut from heavy-stock paper as an alternative to traditional pine or cedar garlands. Or, Thomas states, “Mid- to high-tier retailers like CB2 and West Elm use modern shapes and materials to create some very unique and trendy garlands, like one made of crystal shapes and another with gold-frosted palm fronds.”.

Metallics are a fun, nontraditional way to set an icy winter scene in your space this holiday scene.

It has been revealed that “Metallics can add a sophisticated touch to holiday decor,” states Houston-based interior designer Chandos Dodson Epley of Chandos Collective. “Gold, silver, and bronze create a beautiful shimmer and can be combined with various colors for a modern twist. Pairing metallics with whites and deep greens can really elevate the festive atmosphere.” Plus metallics work well with Fresh Year’s Eve trimmings, for those who like to let their Christmas decorations linger a bit.

You only need a few tasteful figurines to transform an ordinary tabletop into a holiday-themed vignette.

Sources indicate that sticking to one tone for trinkets artfully arranged on a console table or windowsill is a way to add holiday cheer that doesn’t look too busy. Add candles to your window display for an inviting glow that guests can spot as they come up your walkway. For the actual windows, Maggie Griffin of Maggie Griffin Design in Gainesville, Georgia, says nothing tops a traditional wreath. “I love a simple magnolia or boxwood wreath with a long silk ribbon with an understated bow. It’s classic and simple!” she says.

Repurposing leftover upholstery into stocking is a fun, easy DIY project.

If you’ve recently reupholstered, use leftover fabric scraps to create stockings that pair perfectly with your furniture. Or eyeball your existing chairs and couches and try to make a match. The room seen here—with walls painted Aubusson Blue by Annie Sloan—has striped stockings that make even the non-seasonal decor (the chairs) look more cohesive and intentional. Sloan takes the idea a step farther by matching her presents too. The chair, stockings, and gift wrap are all done in Sloan’s Ticking in Olive fabric.

Recent findings suggest that no space for a 9-foot tree indoors? Try decking out a plant.

Designer Bailey Todd of White Cliff Studio in Columbus, Illinois, supports the desire to have multiple Christmas trees, or a decked-out tree and plant combo. “If you have lots of indoor tropical plants in your living room and don’t want to (or can’t) move them, decorate those too,” she notes. “Just be sure not to use any heavy decor—keep garlands and ornaments light so you don’t damage any stems.” For a modern spin that’s also ideal for small spaces, skip the evergreen altogether and just go for the potted plant.

No need to completely change the palette of your space just to get it holiday-ready.

In a recent development, greenfeld is a fan of a beautiful garland draped across the mantel. “When the garland gently hangs over the edges, it creates a soft, organic feel that perfectly frames the mantel and adds elegance without overwhelming the space,” he notes. But doing so doesn’t mean you have to ditch your living room’s current, non-holiday color scheme. “I always suggest incorporating colors that complement the room so the garland enhances the space rather than compete with it.”.

Recent findings suggest that subtlety not your thing? Go maximalist this Christmas with a themed tree.

“This year’s holiday decor is all about natural elegance and emotional warmth,” declares designer Anita Yokota, who decked the halls of the White House in 2023. “Real greenery, organic textures, and soft metallics create calm, layered spaces that feel alive.” Here, she’s adorned a tree in more muted, earthy tones alongside ornaments inspired by nature, like mushrooms. Golden accents complement all the browns and tans on the tree, adding just a touch of glamour.

DIY garland making can be a fun holiday activity at home for the whole family.

Sources indicate that “I love when holiday decor feels gathered, not purchased,” says Jessica Whitley of Jessica Whitley Studio in Athens, Georgia. “Here, olive and rosemary branches bring sculptural softness to [the mantel’s] dark marble. A few metallic touches, like vintage bells or subtle shimmered ribbon catch the light and make the greenery feel festive without overpowering the space.”.

A Christmas village—especially one that doubles as cozy mood lighting—is one way outside of your typical wreaths and trees to lend your home some holiday cheer.

According to recent reports, every surface serves as an opportunity to introduce some festive flair, as seen with this hallway table designed by Renae. Creating a Christmas village is a fun way for little ones to help with DIY Christmas decorations; they can paint buildings (available at craft shops or dollar stores like Dollar Tree) and even mold holiday-themed figurines, like a reindeer and or snowman, from clay. Keeping decor cozy and nostalgic aligns with this year’s trends, according to Renae. “For 2025, I’m all about the cozy, nostalgic vibe of Christmas,” she tells AD. “I love classic plaids, deep reds, and those warm, comforting touches that make any space feel like you’ve stepped into a Christmas movie.”.

One simple method of giving your home a dash of holiday happiness? Add a simple runner in red-and-green plaid.

An easy way to weave holiday home decor into unexpected spaces is through rugs. Roll out a mat, runner, or larger carpet for a quick and cozy look. “Seasonal motifs, such as garlands, reindeer, or plaid, instantly make a space feel warm and festive for holiday gatherings,” says Maria O’Brien of Ruggable. Or opt for a yuletide spin on plaid, like a timeless tartan, as seen above. “Heritage-inspired patterns are having a moment, with classic red and green tones adding a touch of tradition to the home,” says O’Brien.

Bells and bows are tried-and-true Christmas classics.

Though model and actor Kara Del Toro lives in Los Angeles, she wanted her home to have a European feel for the holidays. “With our German roots, my mom and grandmother always brought little European touches into our holiday traditions,” she notes. “So this year, I wanted to bring that nostalgia and old-world charm into my own home with a quaint European Christmas that complemented its Mediterranean architecture rather than competing with it.” To do so, she sourced cedar, pine, noble fir, olive branches, asparagus fern, red astilbe, and other seasonal flora to make her own garlands. She then added bells and red bows, embellishments you could picture at a Christmas market in Germany.

Pinecones, pomegranates, and oranges add some life to this festive tablescape.

According to recent reports, to carrying that old-world feel over to her dining table, Del Toro decided to festoon it with fruit. “I layered all of the greenery with pears, pomegranates, dried orange slices, and pinecones, then added loads of candles for a little sparkle,” she says. “I love how something as simple as fruit or a beautiful branch can feel so festive when you put it all together.”.

Exploring alternative options to your traditional Christmas tree? Think outside the box: Most greenery looks merry wrapped in lights and red bows.

If you already have a tree or large plant in your living room, make it the main attraction, like Del Toro did here. “One of my favorite decisions was skipping a traditional Christmas tree altogether,” she claims. “I have an 18-foot olive tree named Olivia in my living room, and she’s already the focal point of the space. I thought, why compete with her? Instead, I climbed up on my ladder and dressed her with antique-style bells, twinkling lights, and hand-tied bows. It feels so fitting for a Mediterranean home, and I love that it’s a little unexpected.”.

Embroidered napkins can add a festive flair to any holiday party.

It has been revealed that if you’re hosting a holiday soirée, an embroidered cocktail napkin—like these, part of a 12 Days of Christmas set from Lettermade—is a small touch that makes a substantial impact, since your guests will be sitting with and handling them all night. Tying bows around the stems of your glassware is an equally charming detail.

It has been revealed that even if you go substantial for holiday decor, you don’t have to go against the grain. Tap into your existing color palette and style for Christmas decor if you’re craving a cohesive look.

“When decorating for the holidays, I like to build on the warmth and character of a home by incorporating rich, natural colors like olive, moss and burgundy that complement the existing interiors,” says Jennifer Sissom of Ryan Street Architects in Austin. Here, the team at Ryan Street did just that by mixing in hues that match year-round artwork in jewelry designer Kendra Scott’s Austin home.

Glassy ornaments make for a sleek winter wonderland.

Recent findings suggest that in Scott’s home, the tree is decked with retro-looking mercury glass ornaments. “Looking ahead to holiday trends for 2026, I’m seeing a continued appreciation for vintage and collected pieces, particularly antique ornaments and aged mercury glass, which bring a softness and sense of history to holiday decorating,” states Sissom. “Overall, there’s a shift toward more personal, layered spaces that feel timeless rather than overly seasonal.”.

What are 2026’s top trends in Christmas decor?

Recent findings suggest that “This year, the holiday decor trends are grounded in a beautiful balance between nostalgia, whimsy, and sophistication,” says designer Taniya Nayak, a Marshalls and TJ Maxx home style expert. “We're seeing a continued appreciation for timeless holiday pieces, but with more personality, rich textures, and unexpected color combinations. It’s less about following a specific aesthetic and more about creating a home that feels festive, warm, and collected over time.”.

While minimalism has had its moment in recent years, Nayak says the trend is shifting toward a more playful, maximalist approach to holiday decorating. “People are embracing more whimsical details like gingham, bells with luxe velvet bows, graphic black-and-white stripes, festive glassware, plaid throw pillows, or an unexpected accent like a faux pearl Christmas tree topper that adds personality and dimension without making the space feel overly styled,” she says. Rich jewel tones—popular last year—are still on trend this holiday season. Deep burgundies, emerald greens, and touches of gold or silver create a glamorous palette.

Recent findings suggest that “I'm also loving food-inspired holiday decor,” says Nayak. “It's fun, fresh, and especially chic when styled in an elevated way.” This might mean glass-frosted ornaments that take the form of plump strawberries or an ice cream sundae. Sardine tins and shrimp have been especially popular when given the glass ornament treatment. Nayak also recommends decorating with citrus, such as tucking dried orange slices into greenery. “You can even bring this trend to your holiday table decor with pears, pomegranates, candles, and beautiful serving pieces,” she says. See Del Toro’s Christmas tablescape above for an example of festive fruit accents.

When should I decorate for Christmas?

“My number one rule is that there are no rules when it comes to holiday decorating,” says Nayak. “The holidays are such a special time of joy, happiness, and family, so there’s no shame if you love a head start!” Everyone who has already had their Christmas tree up for a month can breathe a collective sigh of relief. That being noted, Nayak also recommends easing into the season and decorating in stages. “You can start introducing cozy textures, scented candles, greenery, and warm lighting in early November. I also personally like to layer in chic serveware and velvet accessories that transition beautifully from Thanksgiving to Christmas. Then, as Thanksgiving approaches or passes, you can bring out more traditional holiday decorations,” she says.

If you're a procrastinator, that’s also perfectly fine.”There’s no deadline for creating a little holiday magic, and you don’t need to splurge or spend weeks decorating to make your home feel magical,” says Nayak.

Whether you’re looking to add small, unique holiday accents, like a beautiful decorative game set, a premium wool blend throw, or a silver-rimmed serving plate that inspires an entire holiday tablescape—or you’re looking to completely overhaul your space into a winter wonderland, it’s nice to have a game strategy before you hit the shops.

According to recent reports, sometimes, a few thoughtful additions are all you need to make your home feel festive. As an added bonus, late decorators can also scoop up deals as holiday decor begins to be marked down.

How do I incorporate holiday decorations in more unexpected places throughout the house?

For those truly obsessed with the Christmas holiday, decorations don’t have to be confined to the living room. As shown above, designers have decked out kitchens, bedrooms, and hallways for the season; Button is even bringing the holiday spirit to her bathrooms. “Each year, I choose a newly introduced space to gussy up with festive decor,” she notes. This year will be the bathrooms as a fun spot. I hide plastic animals with ribbons or mini wreaths on them for my children. It becomes a fun game to discover where the creatures have hidden themselves—sometimes peeking out from the tops of mirrors, or near the towel bar, or by the tub!”.

What are some budget-friendly Christmas decor ideas that look expensive?

In a recent development, “Holiday decor doesn’t have to break the bank,” notes Nayak. Small touches like festive kitchen accessories, tablescape accents, and natural elements such as garlands and wreaths are affordable ways to channel the holiday spirit. By prioritizing timeless, quality decor, you’ll create a well-curated atmosphere that will last for many seasons to come.

Where do I put the Christmas tree?

The centerpiece of holiday home decor is usually the tree, so placement is key. Samantha Stathis Lynch, designer and home style expert with Marshalls and TJ Maxx, indicates, “Christmas trees are often the focal point of holiday decor for those celebrating Christmas, so it’s important to have the tree in a room that is accessible and spacious. The living room or family room is often the most utilized; however, any room in your home can accentuate the tree—it’s all about preference.” Placing your tree in front of a window makes for elegant Christmas decor for your home’s exterior as well. (Is there anything more homey than seeing glowing Christmas lights in a window?) Or place your tree in the living room’s entryway so it can be enjoyed from adjoining rooms and add to your dining room’s ambiance or Christmas kitchen decor.

How can I make my house look cozy?

Sources indicate that A cozy Christmas living room is all about texture, Thomas claims. “Whether that’s velvet drapes, bouclé throw pillow covers, or a high-pile rug, textiles are the perfect way to add diverse textures to a room without making it feel overwhelming.”.

Industry observers note that adding to that, Lynch recommends including subtle lighting, candles, and additional seating around your Christmas tree. “Ottomans or poufs can make any space the perfect area to gather around your tree and celebrate the season,” she says. Temporary seating near a Christmas fireplace is another option. Add throw blankets and trays with hot cocoa mugs to mimic ski chalet vibes. It’ll transform your living room into a cozy spot within a winter wonderland.

How to decorate living room windows for Christmas.

Sources indicate that windows are even more real estate for your Christmas theme. “Symmetry across window panes is a largely popular seasonal trend that can be easily achieved with wreaths, candles, or garland,” Lynch indicates. “Place matching Christmas wreaths within the center of your home’s front-facing windows or candle holders and taper candles within each windowsill for a picturesque holiday home.”.

Thomas, on the other hand, prefers more modern Christmas decor, like acrylic nutcrackers or matte white decorative presents. “Gathering these design-forward yet minimal trinkets in groups of three or five to form triangles—or what designers call three-point thinking—provides depth and intrigue to the eye,” he explains. “Windows are essentially built-in frames in a room. Knowing that, any window decor should lead with composition and proportion first, which is why less will always be more when it comes to windows.”.

How to hang stockings and garlands.

It has been revealed that thomas recommends using Command Clear Hooks for garlands that serve as mantel decor, emphasizing that “these should be in the arsenal of any DIY’er, as they are a great option for temporary solutions.” You could also use a tension rod in a pinch. “I’ve seen some rather creative implementations of this technique where folks will place a tension rod in between a passageway and use that to hang a garland. I will definitely be trying this method this year,” he adds. Before wrapping your garland around the rod, you can even spray-paint it green so it blends in better.

“When it comes to hanging stockings, I’m a traditionalist and I recommend investing in stocking hangers,” Thomas indicates. “These can be used year after year, and with so many options on the market, one can absolutely find an option that suits the rest of the decor. However, not everyone has real estate like a fireplace mantel to hang stockings, so I recommend some damage-free adhesive hooks.”.

Tech Report: Leading Medical Groups Team Up to Redefine Female Heart Health

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated strategy of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.
  • The reports detail how cardiovascular health issues can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.
  • The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated strategy of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.

The reports detail how cardiovascular health issues can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.

The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.

They stress that females have specific biological factors that increase their risks of cardiovascular disease. Those components include hormonal and emotional factors.

It has been revealed that the authors note that heart disease is the number one cause of death for females in the United States, as well as the number one cause of death during pregnancy. Yet, only 44% of females are fully aware of the dangers they face from heart disease.

The organizations issuing the reports are the American Heart Association (AHA), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

The groups presented their findings in a trio of reports published in the AHA’s flagship journal, Circulation on October 26.

“Women experience their healthcare across clinical specialties, but it often is fragmented or disconnected,” mentioned Sadiya Khan, MD, the chair of the collaborative writing group for the reports and a professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago, in a news release.

“Specifically, these reports connect the dots for clinicians, for patients, and across health domains so that care is holistic and begins in adolescence, recognizing that women’s heart health is uniquely shaped by biological transitions not experienced by men — periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and menopause.”.

Experts not involved in the reports told Healthline the updates were a long time coming.

Nicole Weinberg, MD, a cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California, remarked the reports present a positive framework for women’s health.

“Women have unique cardiovascular risk factors related to pregnancy and menopause, and certain traditional risk factors, including diabetes, may increase their risk of heart disease more significantly than they do in men,” noted Nissi Suppogu, MD, a cardiologist and medical director of the Women’s Heart Center at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California.

“Recognizing these differences is essential to identifying women at risk earlier, improving prevention strategies and ensuring they receive appropriate treatment,” she said.

“I am incredibly excited to see these latest reports on women’s heart health,” added Svati Shah, MD, the president-elect of the AHA, as well as the associate dean of Translational Research and the director of Precision Genomics Collaboratory in the Duke School of Medicine in North Carolina.

“They are a call to action for increasing education, research, and coordinated clinical care for women’s heart health,” Shah said.

The organizations spelled out their recommendations in three reports.

The first report is a presidential advisory that lays out a “female-specific life course approach to the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that “girls and women uniquely experience fragmented care” across medical fields, including pediatrics, obstetrics, and gynecology.

The authors call for a “unified life course approach that addresses the female-specific interconnectedness of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health.”.

This report breaks down the life cycle for girls and women into five stages.

“Emerging data suggest that unique biologic transitions or life stages experienced by girls and women are linked with changes in [cardiovascular disease] risk, which may be due in part to physiologic changes in sex hormones,” the authors wrote.

Weinberg said this life-stage breakdown is important, especially for risk reduction.

She noted issues with menstruation during the teen years may be a harbinger of heart health problems later in life. The same is true for health issues during pregnancy, especially high blood pressure or high blood sugar levels.

“We need to be aware of these heart disease risks so we’re not caught by surprise 10 to 20 years down the road,” Weinberg noted.

According to recent reports, suppogu agreed. “Medical professionals should emphasize that heart health is a lifelong priority and prevention should begin early. Encourage girls and women to establish healthy habits, understand their cardiovascular risk factors, and maintain regular checkups, even when they feel healthy.”.

“Women’s heart health has a unique constellation of risk factors and manifestations that are shaped by biological transitions that vary across a woman’s lifetime,” noted Shah.

The second report is a science advisory that recommends a comprehensive strategy for women’s cardiovascular care.

In it, the authors call for a system that “integrates assessment of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across life stages.”.

They propose a “national infrastructure” of centers that would coordinate clinical care, education, training, research, and community engagement around women’s heart health.

Sources indicate that “These centers can reduce fragmentation, enhance earlier risk identification, and expand opportunities to increase representation of women in clinical research,” the authors wrote. “In doing so, they offer a bold opportunity for a scalable and equitable model to improve cardiovascular health for all women.”.

To illustrate their point, the authors noted that only about 60% of women with hypertensive disorders during pregnancy in the United States have a follow-up visit with a healthcare professional about their condition within the first 6 months after giving birth.

“Given that pregnancy is a cardiovascular stress test and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are risk-enhancing factors for long-term [cardiovascular disease] risk, this represents a major missed opportunity to address cardiovascular risk,” the authors wrote.

“Pregnancy and the postpartum period are key windows into cardiovascular health throughout the life course,” stated William Grobman, MD, the vice-chair of the writing group for these reports and a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, in the press release.

“An adverse pregnancy outcome can unmask increased cardiovascular risk, and that information should guide care well beyond pregnancy,” he continued.

The third report is a scientific statement that suggests a “consensus guideline for the female-specific prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that there is “growing recognition that the optimal prevention and management of cardiovascular disease in girls and women requires attention to sex-specific considerations relevant to the interconnected domains of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across the life course.”.

Sources indicate that the authors note several age-related warning signs of heart problems. These are spelled out in the AHA press release.

According to recent reports, females comprise around half the population, and their cardiovascular health “must be a part of everyday care across medicine,” said Mariell Jessup, MD, the chief science and medical officer of the American Heart Association, in the press release. “These publications give clinicians and health systems a shared foundation for recognizing risk throughout a woman’s life.”.

In a scientific statement published in February 2026, the AHA projected that 60% of females in the United States will have at least one type of cardiovascular disease by 2050.

Sources indicate that the organization also predicted that 25% of U.S. women will have diabetes and 60% will have obesity by that year if current trends continue.

The authors of that report listed several steps they mentioned could reverse these trends. Among them:.

Experts say women can also take action on their own to reduce their risks. Suppogu suggests the following:.

These recommendations can also be found in the AHA’s Life’s Essential 8 tips for a healthy heart.

“Most importantly, we need to educate women that heart disease is not inevitable, and early intervention can help prevent it and improve long-term health,” Suppogu stated.

According to recent reports, weinberg advised women to include plenty of fruits and vegetables and a minimal amount of meat in their daily diet. She stated that women should have regular check-ups with their doctor, and that adopting a healthy lifestyle doesn’t have to be complicated.

According to recent reports, khan stated women’s health is a community effort. “All girls and women deserve more healthy years to live their fullest lives,” she said in the press release.

Sources indicate that “Advancing women’s health is a responsibility we all share. This investment improves not only women’s health but also the health of their families and their communities.”.

In bear life, as in human life, sometimes you just have to take a leap of faith. A brown bear (Ursus arctos) cub hanging around Anan Creek in Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska learned that this summer. Its mom, Gemini, was crossing the creek, and one cub jumped right in. But this cub? Not so sure. It stood waiting at the water’s edge, before jumping in.

Industry observers note that for this forceful leap into the water, the park rangers have awarded Gemini’s little cub with the 2026 Yeet of Faith Award. For those keeping score at home, Gemini won this year’s helicopter mom award.

“Cubs learn at their own pace, and thanks to amazing recreation sites like Anan, we get to witness their tiny triumphs up close,” the rangers write.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Sources indicate that tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots for wildlife is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears (Ursus americanus) and eight brown bears like Gemini and her cubs. Similar to their chubby counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to gorge on salmon ahead of the long winter, and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear around Anan Creek has their own habits and quirks.

According to recent reports, the U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behaviors.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • As the holidays approach, you're likely to meet latest people and socialize with colleagues and family you don't normally see the rest of the year.
  • In such settings, you're also more likely to come into situations where you sense a bit of "healthy competition." Turkey Trot, anyone?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

As the holidays approach, you're likely to meet latest people and socialize with colleagues and family you don't normally see the rest of the year.

In such settings, you're also more likely to come into situations where you sense a bit of "healthy competition." Turkey Trot, anyone? You may also interact with people playing the "one-up" game, where someone shares a more intense version of the story or situation you just shared.

Whenever people gather, we're assessing and comparing. Everyone does it. It's natural. It helps us understand how we fit in and get cues on how to behave.

Envy not only can occur, but it can also help you navigate these times...though not in the way most people expect.

When some people discover I've written a book on envy, but they are not yet aware of its contents, they will tell me, "I don't feel envy, but I know a lot of people who do." They will then proceed to tell me about the people who envy them.

Sources indicate that they don't know that I believe that everyone envies. It is a universal emotion. Unpleasant, yes, but not necessarily a harmful one.

In a recent development, I get it. In this culture where envy is often seen as a deadly sin, it's hard to admit feeling envy.

But not acknowledging one's own envy is unfortunate because you miss out on all that envy can reveal to you. However, that isn't the mistake I want to focus on here. I believe the bigger mistake is to assume that you know when someone else is feeling envy.

First, we can't be certain it is envy they are feeling. Not only is it impossible to read minds, but we also can't reliably detect envy from their faces. As envy researcher Jens Lange told me, "If there were [a unique envy facial expression], we would likely suppress it.".

According to recent reports, second, when we ascribe envy to someone else, we create an artificial barrier. We make a negative judgment about their character and lower their status to elevate ourselves. Not even conscious of this, we begin to operate on the false assumption and the distance we've created. It subtly impacts our interactions and our behaviors.

According to recent reports, first, adopt a curious mindset. It's harder to stop your mind from thinking of something than it is to suggest something fresh to consider. So, instead of saying, "Don't judge or make assumptions," try, "I don't know their story." Remind yourself that you don't know what happened in their past, what just happened moments ago, what their circumstances are, or what their mood is.

It has been revealed that second, dial up the warmth. Amy Cuddy, Susan Fiske, and Peter Glick's research revealed that when people encounter one another, they ask two questions: "Does this person want to harm or help me?" and "Is this person capable of following through with their threat or assistance?" They found that people tend to be envied when they are not warm but competent. So, if it is true that you're envied, more reason to approach with warmth.

During your year-end holiday festivities, try combining these two concepts and adopt a "warm curiosity.".

You may walk away learning unexpected reasons why you like someone you didn't before.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to newly introduced research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported. The authors posted the study on a research-sharing website on September 4. Other scientists have not yet peer-reviewed the work.

Charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study. She told Healthline the main takeaway for adults over 50 was that “it’s not too late to try and do things that are going to improve your health.”Nearly half of U.S. adults ages 40 to 59 had obesity from 2021 to 2023, the highest rate of any adult age group, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Among all U.S. adults, around 31.7% were overweight, according to the CDC.

The findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S. adults share similar weight patterns, remarked Solveig Cunningham, PhD, a professor of global health at Emory University’s Rollins School of Public Health. Cunningham, who was not involved in the research, told Healthline that Americans tend to gain weight across adulthood.

“By the time you get into your 50s, close to the majority of Americans already have obesity. Many others have overweight,” she remarked.The World Health Organization (WHO) calls obesity a chronic disease. Healthcare professionals diagnose overweight and obesity using a person’s weight and height, or body mass index (BMI).

Bridger-Staatz mentioned the team set out to learn who lost weight and kept it off before GLP-1 weight loss medications became available, and whether that weight loss improved health over time.

It has been revealed that she remarked researchers had long assumed that “once people had become overweight or developed obesity, people didn’t really lose weight and certainly not sustained it.”The team also asked, she said, “can we try and say something positive about health that isn’t just this kind of like doom and gloom?”The researchers used the British 1958 National Child Development Study, which has followed about 17,500 people born during one week in 1958. Of those, 6,309 took part in a health check in their early 60s, according to the report.The team compared each person’s highest weight between ages 23 and 42 with their weight between ages 50 and 55. Researchers sorted people by whether they gained or lost more than 5% of their body weight and kept the change. For a 200-pound person, 5% equals 10 pounds.To track heart health, the team compared blood tests and blood pressure readings at ages 44 and 62 with those of people who maintained a healthy weight.“We know everyone’s heart health is kind of going to get a little bit worse over that time because you are aging and that’s expected,” Bridger-Staatz said. The question, she said, was, “Does it slow the rate at which people’s heart health is getting worse?”.

Sources indicate that weight loss slowed the decline in heart health for people who were overweight and for people with obesity, according to the report.People who were overweight and lost weight had the strongest positive results. By age 62, their body fat-to-lean tissue ratio matched that of the healthy-weight group. The authors wrote that differences in body fat may partly explain why weight changes affected heart health.People with obesity who lost weight had less body fat at 62 than people in the other obesity groups, according to the report.Sudhakara Chennareddy, MD, prevention cardiologist in the Center for Cardiovascular Prevention, Metabolism and Lipids at Georgia Heart Institute, told Healthline those results are what he’d expect. He was not involved in the research.“Even losing 5% has beneficial effects on the cardiovascular side effects,” he stated. Long-term blood sugar was the exception. For people with obesity who lost weight, it rose more than in the healthy-weight group, though the authors reported that the result was not statistically significant.

A 2025 study of more than 15,000 U.S. adults, published in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism, found that adults who had previously had obesity tended to have higher blood sugar than those who had never had it, even after their BMI dropped.

In a recent development, “It’s not the patient’s fault… We need to treat this one like any other chronic disease, like we treat hypertension or we treat diabetes,” Chennareddy said.Compared with the healthy-weight group, people who gained weight in their early 50s had faster increases in blood pressure, blood fats, and inflammation, and declines in “good” cholesterol. Obesity is a chronic metabolic disease that leads to inflammation in the body, which can raise the risk of heart attack and stroke and worsen cholesterol levels, Chennareddy said. “The more weight they gain, they develop prediabetes and diabetes and fatty liver disease as well,” he said.These changes were largest for people who developed obesity or already had obesity and gained more weight, the researchers reported. This group also saw faster increases in long-term blood sugar levels.About 37% of participants gained more than 5% of their body weight in their early 50s. Only about 6% lost weight and kept it off, according to the study.“To me, that’s sort of the stronger message,” Cunningham said of the findings. Her advice for adults in their 50s is to avoid gaining weight.

People with obesity who lost and then gained the weight back saw faster drops in “good” cholesterol and faster rises in inflammation and long-term blood sugar.

By age 62, they weighed slightly less, on average, than people whose obesity remained steady, according to the report’s data. They also carried more body fat and had more inflammation.Weight cycling can do more harm than steady weight, Chennareddy stated. He gave the example of someone who gains 20 pounds, loses 30 and then gains 20 again. “That is even more detrimental,” he said.When people lose weight, the body slows its resting metabolism, he said. When the weight comes back, “most of the weight they gain is fat, not muscle,” he said. Even someone who loses and regains 5% to 7% of their body weight may end up with slightly less muscle and more fat, he said.Some research has shown that weight fluctuation is associated with a higher risk of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease-related death.

The study’s weight changes took place between about 2008 and 2013, according to the study’s timeline.

Wegovy, a GLP-1 medication for weight management, launched in the United Kingdom in September 2023, according to the UK Department of Health and Social Care.Cunningham said the weight-cycling findings raised questions for people who take GLP-1 medications. She said drugmakers’ own data show that “once you get off of those, your weight is going to go right back to where it was before, possibly even worse.”That could create the same up-and-down pattern, Cunningham said. She added that researchers don’t yet know “what happens in the really long term” for people who take these medications.

The study showed links between weight changes and heart health and cannot prove that weight changes caused the results, according to the authors. They wrote that the small number of people who lost weight made those results less precise.Bridger-Staatz also stated the team did not look at why or how people lost weight.

In a recent development, cunningham said adults lose muscle and bone mass with age, and that the loss is especially pronounced for women in their 50s and older. “Maintaining muscles and maintaining bones is so, so crucial,” she said.Staying active helps people keep muscle, even without weight loss, Cunningham said. “Even a little bit of activity…just keep moving,” she said.GLP-1 medications work best as part of a “comprehensive initiative,” Chennareddy said. With his patients, he said he recommends continuous improvement rather than setting a goal to lose a specific amount of weight within a set period.Patients who treat weight loss as “a gradual process” do better long term, he said.“The most important thing is not to do fad diets,” Chennareddy said.For people losing weight, Chennareddy recommended:.

Anyone considering changes to their weight can talk with a healthcare professional about their weight history and goals.

The 10 Best Hiking Backpacks, Tested by Outdoor Gear Editors

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A GOOD HIKING backpack is just as important—if not more so—as a good pair of hiking boots, hiking shoes, or any other hiking gear.
  • Finding the right backpack for you can be like shopping for the perfect mattress.
  • Winner of this year’s “Best New All-Purpose Backpack” in the latest Men’s Health Outdoor Awards, the Kestrel LT 45 is the bag to buy if you only want to buy one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A GOOD HIKING backpack is just as important—if not more so—as a good pair of hiking boots, hiking shoes, or any other hiking gear. Whether you're venturing deep into the backcountry or exploring a local trail, your pack will be strapped to your back for an extended period of time. It needs to be reliable, comfortable, durable, and offer the right storage and organization options to suit your style of hiking. Oh, and affordability is a nice-to-have, too.

Finding the right backpack for you can be like shopping for the perfect mattress. Backpack technology isn't what it used to be when your grandpappy was hitting the trail. It's far better but also a lot more complicated. You'll need to understand frame types and nylon fabric densities and hydration system compatibilities and—well, you get the picture. It's all just a little more confusing than it needs to be. That's why our expert team put together this guide to the best hiking backpacks to help you find the perfect pack without breaking your back and the bank in the process.

Winner of this year’s “Best New All-Purpose Backpack” in the latest Men’s Health Outdoor Awards, the Kestrel LT 45 is the bag to buy if you only want to buy one. It’s Osprey’s reimagining of the classic rucksack design. It’s rugged yet lightweight, with a 45-liter capacity that’s more than enough for most hikers on all but the longest multiday treks. I personally love the streamlined exterior that cinches down tight for maximum compression. Osprey’s AirScape back panel offers just-right cushioning, coupled with simple torso-length adjustability to fit a wide range of body shapes and sizes.

Sources indicate that after months of testing, this has consistently proven to be my go-to pack for most hikes because everything about it just works. Plus, the price point hits the midrange sweet spot, ensuring it’s affordable enough for most, even for first-time hiking backpack buyers on a budget. Bonus: An attached rain cover is included.

In a recent development, at just 12 liters and weighing only 390 grams, this pack is designed for ultra-efficient climbs and lightning-fast summit assaults. It's the daypack you grab when most other daypacks are too much. I found the simple organizational layout—one main compartment and two zippered pockets (one internal, one external)—made wrangling my day hiking essentials a breeze. Additional gear loops at the rear provide extra space for hanging anything you might need at the ready. The just-right back padding, removable hip belt, and ventilated mesh shoulder straps were extremely comfy for tackling daily summits in the White Mountains.

Industry observers note that it's all made from recycled, eco-friendly materials that are Bluesign certified, with a PFC-free DWR treatment. The best part? It's among the most affordable brand-name speedpacks we'd recommend this year.

Read More: How We Pack Hiking Backpacks.

Like every Gregory pack I've tested in the last two decades, the Paragon 60 is durable, cleverly designed, and features smart organizational options. But I'm including it here mainly because it's so dang comfy to wear. It features a widely adjustable torso length and an airy mesh back panel that breathes well thanks to a design that's 90 percent air. The hip belt is equally adjustable, too, with dynamic panels that move independently of the frame. Translation: It's the most comfortable pack I tested this year, even after hundreds of miles of hiking with fairly heavy loads.

Bonus: The PFAS-free durable water-repellent (DWR) coating on the body, bottom, and pack lining means it's more eco-friendly, too.

Read More: Best Cold-Weather Hiking Gear.

Yeti’s first foray into the hardcore hiking backpack game comes on the heels of its recent acquisition of the Mystery Ranch brand. The Skala is a deft combination of Mystery Ranch’s legendary design prowess and Yeti’s built-to-survive-anything durability. The former’s RipZip opening is the star of this pack, providing instant access to its contents with a quick one-handed pull. The Skala features multiple adjustment points and a clever load distribution system that combine to ensure a perfect fit and all-day comfort on the trail.

True to the Yeti brand, it's packed with premium, heavy-duty materials built to survive years of abuse. The only downsides? At 3.4 pounds, it’s heavier than many in this weight class. It’s also pricier than most of its competition. But if you’re a fan of Yeti and/or MR and don’t mind the “buy once, cry once” price point, this is definitely worth considering.

Read More: Yeti Skala Backpack Review.

For an all-in-one solution—a backpack that moves effortlessly from your morning commute to the office to the trail and back again—Peak Design's new Outdoor 25L pack delivers. The frameless, low-profile build is extremely comfy on and off the trail. The brand's signature organizational elements are here, too—it's hydration system-compatible, features a 16-inch laptop sleeve, and is purpose-built to accept PD's own gear cubes (sold separately) so you can divvy up the main compartment however you see fit. The drawstring/roll-top closure provides quick and easy access to the internal compartment while protecting your gear from the elements. Fair warning, though: You'll pay a premium for the PD brand name. If you’re looking to size up, the Outdoor Backpack is also available as a more generous 45-liter option.

Mountain Hardwear is upending the ultralight backpacking game with the debut of the all-upcoming Alakazam series. The 45-liter model won a coveted spot in this year’s Men’s Health Outdoor Awards. At just 820 grams, it’s absurdly lightweight with a trail-friendly fit that feels like wearing nothing at all. Yet, it offers enough room for both gear-heavy day hikes and overnights. It’s all thanks to the bleeding-edge ALUULA shell fabric, which is not only light but extremely durable. The storage and organization (with plenty of loops, pockets, and oversized stash pouches) are cleverly laid out, and the unique GiddyUp compression system allows you to cinch your load down on the go. I also especially love the roll-top design that makes the entire bag waterproof. (A 60-liter option is also available.).

Read More: Testing the Alakazam 45.

It has been revealed that like many Arc'teryx packs, the Alpha FL30 is first and foremost built for climbing (including a top strap, six lash points, and a built-in RECCO reflector for SAR situations). But, I also found its sleek silhouette and featherweight construction great for fast-packing. It's only as heavy as it needs to be while still protecting your gear with the brand's own abrasion-resistant Hadron grid fabric. The drawstring opening provides quick access to a cavernous, open-concept interior with only a single, small zippered security pocket.

In a recent development, it's a no-frills design with minimal organization options that won't please every hiker. But it's a solid, if pricey, option for hard-charging trail lovers who appreciate a pack that stays out of its own way.

It has been revealed that with a 44-liter capacity, the Talon 44 is large enough for two-day weekender trips and even longer multiday treks. It's an ideal bag for most hikers looking to buy just one backpack that does it all. I love the slim profile, excellent padding, and close-to-body fit—all of which makes for more comfortable wear, especially after long days on the trail.

Industry observers note that this iteration of Osprey's bestseller features a long list of upgrades to the straps, padding, and overall design. Plus, I found the sheer number of storage options to be perfect for almost any length of trip.

I’ve been a fan of Gossamer Gear’s featherweight fastpacker-friendly gear for years. The Grit 28 is my go-to for fast day hikes and quick summit assaults where I’m willing to trade comfort and convenience for speed. At just over a pound, the 28-liter pack is streamlined and sized right. The storage options are limited, ensuring you pack only what you need and nothing more.

In a recent development, what sets it apart from most of its competition is the vest-style shoulder and sternum straps that wear more like a racing vest for maximum all-day comfort. Despite its light weight, it’s made from two ultra-durable fabrics that I’ve found stand up to plenty of trail abuse.

The Crossroads 27L Carry-On is, first and foremost, a travel backpack (it fits under most airline seats, making it a great carry-on backpack). But Yeti bakes in plenty of trail-ready durability to make this one good enough for hiking, too. The 700-denier TuffSkin Nylon exterior is both water- and abrasion-resistant, with an extra durable and easy-to-clean PU-coated base. Contoured, EVA-foam shoulder straps and a no-pressure back panel make for easy carrying, even during long layovers.

It has been revealed that plus, with a suspended laptop sleeve and multiple zippered pockets inside and out, this has become my go-to weekender bag, especially on trips where I'm intent on hitting the trail straight from the airport. (Pro tip: Pair it with Yeti's own Crossroads packing cubes for maximum organization options.).

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, every hiking backpack is designed for hauling "stuff." The amount of stuff each pack can carry—its capacity—is measured in liters (L) or cubic inches. The right size for you depends on how long you typically hike for (hours, days, weeks?) and how heavy a packer you are. If you're shopping for your first pack, finding the perfect capacity can involve a little trial and error. But for a wide variety of hikers, the following numbers are a good starting point.

If you tend to pack light, the right capacity for you may fall closer to the lower end of the above ranges. If you're an over-packer (no shame!), consider sizing up to a slightly larger pack with a capacity on the upper end of the above ranges. Again: Trial and error.

You may have heard an old hiker's adage that goes something like, "Ounces make pounds, and pounds make pain." It's a simple axiom, but it's true: The more weight you carry, the more work you need to do on the trail. That's why it's important to pack as light as possible while still taking all the essentials. It helps to start with as light a hiking backpack as you can afford. The difference between three pounds and four pounds might not seem like much when you're standing in your living room, but I promise you'll feel every gram of that one-pound difference after 10 miles.

There are three main types of backpack construction: internal frame, external frame, and frameless. External frame packs have largely been phased out in the mainstream outdoor gear space in favor of internal frame models. True to the name, they feature a rigid structure that's "hidden" inside the pack's back panel. They sit closer to the back, hugging the body for a more streamlined fit that's ultimately more comfortable. All but the smallest hiking backpacks we recommend below rely on an internal frame construction.

According to recent reports, some compact daypacks (usually 20 liters or less) use a frameless construction similar to standard school backpacks. The lack of a frame means they're not ideal for supporting heavier loads, but that typically isn't an problem if you're only carrying enough for an afternoon hike. Without a frame, most of these packs collapse down almost completely flat, making them perfect travel backpacks.

In a recent development, some packs—particularly those designed for alpine climbers—rely on top-loading-only designs. Think of a typical shopping bag where the contents are only accessible directly through the top opening. It's simple but limiting. Thankfully, many of the best hiking backpacks these days are accessible via both top and side openings. For larger packs, this makes it infinitely easier to get to the gear at the bottom of your pack without having to take everything out first.

Recent findings suggest that the "best" storage layout is personal to each hiker. If you're an organizational nerd (I count myself among this camp), you may prefer more pockets to better wrangle your gear in a way that makes sense to you. On the other end of the spectrum are alpine-style bags that typically trade more pockets (and zippers and stitching) for a simpler, lighter-weight design. These tend to feature a single open-concept storage compartment with only one or two smaller storage pockets.

A few pieces of gear you want to pack in your hiking backpack include: a hydration bladder, water bottle(s), a phone (with easy access to its camera), a satellite messenger, and bear spray. Most modern bags also offer external storage options, like reinforced crampon patches and gear loops or "daisy chains" (i.e., webbing stitched into the pack's exterior that provides multiple attachment points for wet gear, ice axes, helmets, and more that you may not want to store inside your pack).

Modern hiking backpacks can be deceptively complex, and there are dozens of technical features available on many of today's best models. If you're shopping for anything other than a daypack, consider a bag with a dedicated sleeping bag compartment and sleeping pad straps. For longer treks where you may want to venture away from base camp once you set up your tent, a removable daypack (sometimes the "brain" or top lid of a larger pack converts into an ultra-compact hip bag for this purpose), and a rain cover, which may be a stand-alone piece of fabric with a stretch seam or sewn into the pack itself, so you can easily pull it over the pack if the weather turns south.

As an outdoors writer, I spend countless weeks outside each year. During that time, I've put the most popular and well-reviewed hiking backpacks to the test to determine the best of the best. Over the last 12 months, I've tested dozens of packs from Mystery Ranch, Gossamer Gear, Gregory, Osprey, and more throughout the U.S., in Utah's national parks, the White Mountains of Fresh Hampshire, the vast deserts of Massive Bend National Park, and beyond. I also consulted with Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower on top options, research, and some of his own personal testing. While testing hiking backpacks, I've been sure to take thorough notes on comfort, ease of packing, weight, durability, how well (or not) the weight is spread throughout, and how much gear can fit in them.

So, whether you're looking for a featherweight daypack for afternoon peak-bagging or a full-fledged expedition pack for tackling the wilds of Patagonia, we've got you covered with the 10 best hiking backpacks for any trail.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that after 16 years of painstaking work, the National Archives and its collaborators have finally completed digitizing over 90,000 pension applications submitted to the United States government following the War of 1812. The project is more than just preservation for preservation’s sake. The roughly 2.8 million pages contain long-forgotten and missing details about 19th century Americans, their families, and their everyday lives.

It has been revealed that while archivists previously digitized a similar collection related to the American Revolutionary War, the new documents will help fill in knowledge gaps between early 19th century military events and the 1850 federal census. Patricia Oxley, president of the Federation of Genealogical Societies (FGS), explained the project was also incredibly time-sensitive.

“In the specific case of the War of 1812 pension records, there is an added priority due to their frail state where not acting may mean sacrificing these for future generations,” Oxley noted in a recent announcement.

According to recent reports, the somewhat new United States of America declared war on the United Kingdom on June 18, 1812, citing objections to trade restrictions with France amid the Napoleonic Wars, as well as the Royal Navy’s impressment of American sailors. Although the conflict famously included a British attack on Washington D.C. that resulted in the burning of the White House and U.S. Capitol, little shifted geopolitically between the two nations following the ratification of the Treaty of Ghent on February 17, 1815. The U.S. tallied around 15,000 casualties, while the U.K. and Canada saw about 10,700 deaths. Another 9,000 Indigenous fighters died while enlisted between the two sides.

It has been revealed that today’s military records are meticulously documented and stored digitally, but applying for benefits such as pensions was a much more labor-intensive process during the 19th century. With the burden of proof on each applicant, veterans were required to supply lengthy accounts of their service. Each War of 1812 pension file is liable to contain not just combat information, but the names and personal details of fellow soldiers, family members, spouses, and countless other relations.

“Our owners have been asking for the War of 1812 pension records for some time, and I expect this collection to be very popular based on the rich war time detail it contains,” added Brian Hansen, general manager at Fold3, Ancestry’s military records service and National Archives collaborator.

The collection also includes a full-text search feature using handwriting recognition technology. This lets customers explore the files based on every named individual, and not simply the primary veteran applicants. The pension records are right now available for free on Fold3’s website, and are being added to the National Archives catalog on a rolling basis.

It has been revealed that correction 11/20/26 9:30 a.m. EST: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated the pension archive contained around 7 million files. This was based on an initial assessment from researchers in 2010. The article has been updated to reflect the more accurate tally.

How do I keep my vibrator clean?

According to recent reports, “With any vibrator you’re using, you’re going to want to make sure you’re cleaning it after every session,” Richmond explains. A dirty vibrator can hold bacteria and germs—which, needless to say, can seriously kill the mood.

Recent findings suggest that if you don’t have a sex toy-specific cleanser on hand, you can always use mild soap and warm water to clean your products, states Mintz. Some toys are even dishwasher-safe. But she recommends investing in an ultra-gentle cleanser that’s designed for sex toys. Plus, she notes, they’re easy to use: “You spray them on, leave them to sit, and then wipe them off.” Just make sure your toy is fully dry before you put it away.

Finally, if you have a collection of pleasure products, store them separately, Mintz warns. If you forget to clean one vibrator and then toss it in a bag with several other sex toys, the germs and bacteria can spread to your other products.

Sex-positive, sex toy-specific online stores such as Lovehoney, Babeland, and Good Vibrations are always great places to start, states Mintz. “I would recommend going to a reputable sex shop that has [customer] reviews,” she says.

Depending on where you live, you might also opt to shop for a product in person, notes Laino. “It can be a really fun experience to go to a sex store and look at toys,” she explains, adding that it can also be a great bonding activity with a group of friends or a partner.

High-quality vibrators can be expensive—often, over $100—but there’s a reason you’re shelling out the big bucks. “In general, I would say splurge for a pricier vibrator,” Richmond explains. “Quality control can make a really big difference, and spending a little bit more money is probably going to mean your vibrator will last longer, and have more functional capabilities.”.

Generally speaking, expensive products are usually made from better, more body-safe materials. They also have more special features that will seriously enhance your playtime. “With something cheap, the material might be porous, and it might have only one speed or two,” states Richmond. “Something more expensive will be less porous, maybe waterproof, and have more functionality with speeds, Bluetooth connections, things like that.”.

In a recent development, ultimately, “a good-quality vibrator from a good-quality manufacturer is a good investment,” claims Mintz. That mentioned, it’s okay to try a few mid-priced toys of different categories before splurging on your latest go-to luxury product, she adds.

#201487. Electric cars are finally mainstream in GTA 6, and Vice City is full of them

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1350 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Electric cars are finally mainstream in GTA 6, and Vice City is full of them

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1350 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, electric vehicles have finally gone mainstream in Grand Theft Auto.
  • In a recent development, it’s a big change for a series that spent over a decade treating EVs as a Tesla joke.
  • In a recent development, I’ve been playing GTA 6 since it debuted on Thursday, partly for fun and partly because I wanted to see how Rockstar would handle EVs this time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, electric vehicles have finally gone mainstream in Grand Theft Auto. In GTA 6, EVs are just part of everyday traffic in Vice City, from Tesla and Porsche lookalikes to a parody of Electrify America’s charging network.

In a recent development, it’s a big change for a series that spent over a decade treating EVs as a Tesla joke. After a few days of playing, I’d say Rockstar nailed the vibe.

In a recent development, I’ve been playing GTA 6 since it debuted on Thursday, partly for fun and partly because I wanted to see how Rockstar would handle EVs this time. The answer: a lot better than I expected.

The game starts you in the Keys, Rockstar’s take on the Florida Keys, and it’s a rougher part of Leonida. Lots of older cars and beaters, and you won’t see many EVs.

That changes as you head north to Vice City, the game’s version of Miami. The closer you get, the more electric cars show up in traffic, and the more charging stations you pass. By the time you’re in the city, EVs are just normal cars.

That’s pretty much how EV adoption looks in the real world, concentrated in big, wealthier metro areas while rural areas lag behind.

Here’s what I’ve run into so far:.

That last one got me. Gas cars blocking chargers has been a complaint for as long as public charging has existed, and we’ve covered EV owners blocking a gas station in protest over ICEing. Rockstar recreating it tells me someone at the studio has actually tried to charge an EV in public. Probably even in Florida, which they tried to recreate here.

GTA 6 is the first mainline GTA where energy matters. Gas cars burn fuel and need a pump, and EVs have a battery level and need a plug.

In a recent development, rockstar could have used that to make EVs a pain. It didn’t. In my testing, the EVs have about the same range as the gas cars, charge just as fast as a fill-up, and cost the same or less to top up.

Kotaku’s range test backs that up. On the same highway loop, a Tesla Model 3 lookalike lasted 20 minutes and 23 seconds on a charge, longer than the Banshee sports car at 18 minutes and 31 seconds, and not far off an old pickup at 29 minutes and 8 seconds. Crossing the whole map by highway takes under 15 minutes, according to Kotaku.

And finding a charger isn’t a problem. Wccftech counted 120 EV chargers marked on the map, against just 57 gas stations.

Sources indicate that rockstar’s EV history starts with Coil, the series’ Tesla stand-in, named after the Tesla coil. GTA V, released in 2013, gave us the Coil Voltic, a copy of the original Lotus-based Tesla Roadster, alongside oddballs like the Cheval Surge and the Fisker Karma-inspired Khamelion.

The Voltic was quick off the line and slow everywhere else. It had the lowest top speed of any supercar in the game, which fan lore pins on its battery overheating at speed. That’s pretty much how a lot of people thought about EVs in 2013.

According to recent reports, GTA Online added more electric cars starting in late 2017: the Rimac-inspired Coil Cyclone, then the Model S-based Coil Raiden and the Taycan-inspired Pfister Neon around the Doomsday Heist patch. That same update introduced Avon Hertz, a tech billionaire whose AI tries to end the world. Rockstar never stated who he was based on. Players didn’t need the help.

Sources indicate that but those were rare, expensive toys. Nothing in GTA V needed fuel, so an EV was just a gas car without the engine noise, and you mostly saw them in the garages of players who bought them.

Sources indicate that electrify America noticed its in-game twin fast. The Volkswagen-owned network put out a statement on Friday saying it “will stick to charging vehicles in the real world” and adding, “We wish ReVolt America well.”.

It’s a good-natured response, and probably the best free marketing the network has had in years. EA has spent most of the last decade fighting a reputation for broken chargers, even though reliability across US fast-charging networks has improved this year. Every ReVolt station I’ve used in the game worked. Not a perfect parody, then.

Industry observers note that GTA has always been a parody of American life. With EVs, it’s now slightly ahead of it.

Sources indicate that florida is one of the strongest EV markets in the country, with a 9.4% share of new passenger vehicle sales in Q2 2026 versus 7.4% nationally, according to the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy. Electrify America alone runs more than 350 chargers at over 60 Florida stations, including its biggest station yet near Orlando’s theme parks.

In a recent development, but real Florida still has roughly three gas stations for every public charging location, based on the Alliance for Automotive Innovation’s count of 3,267 charging locations and xMap’s count of more than 10,500 gas stations. Leonida flips that ratio.

Sources indicate that there’s one piece Rockstar hasn’t nailed, at least not yet. You can’t install a charger at your place, but early in the story you’re renting. I’m not far enough in to own a property, so I don’t know whether that changes later.

Recent findings suggest that it matters, because home charging is the biggest real-world advantage of an EV. Most owners leave every morning with a full battery and rarely use public chargers. If owned properties in GTA 6 come with a plug, EVs become the more convenient choice in the game, just like they are in real life for anyone with a driveway.

Sources indicate that I also haven’t hit a mission built around EVs yet. If I find one, I’ll enhancement this post.

GTA works as a mirror. In 2013, the EV was a punchline: a Tesla parody that overheated if you drove it too fast. In 2026, it’s just another car in Vice City traffic, and the joke is on the guy in the pickup parked in the charging stall.

It has been revealed that that’s a good sign of where EVs actually are. Satire goes after what’s common, and Rockstar decided EVs are common enough to be part of everyday Leonida, more so in the city than in the Keys, just like real life. And that message is reaching a huge audience. Take-Two claims GTA 6 did $3.79 billion in first-day sales. Tens of millions of people are now driving EVs that charge as fast and as cheaply as gas cars, with no range anxiety. No automaker ad campaign gets close to that.

So EVs aren’t a statement in GTA anymore. They’re normal, which is exactly the point the industry has been trying to make for years.

The real Florida just needs to catch up.
